BOI.name: Boise
BOI.excerpt: Unsettled conditions continue as the upper-level low moves east of the area Friday, bringing northwesterly flow aloft and light showers.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Another round of rain and snow Wednesday through Friday.
- Accumulating snow Wednesday morning will impact roads in SE Oregon. Higher southern mountains will see moderate to locally heavy snowfall totals through Friday.
- The pattern remains cool and unsettled through early next week.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: After brief clearing this evening, clouds will increase later tonight as the next storm pushes onto the coast. A warm front will extend into SE Oregon early Wednesday, weakening as it lifts into central Idaho during day. Southeast Oregon will see the best chance for accumulating snow on Wednesday. Lower basins/valleys in northern Harney and Malheur counties and southern Baker County will see snow develop just before sunrise on Wednesday, impacting Hwy 20 and 26 north/west of Vale. Lower elevations will see up to 2 inches, with 2-5 inches across mtn passes and over higher terrain through Wednesday afternoon.

Precipitation will spread into SW Idaho during the day Wednesday, brining valley rain and mtn snow. Models are consistent tracking the low through northern CA and into northern NV on Thursday which will again place the focus of heavier precipitation and snowfall over our southern mtns to include the Steens, Owyhees, southern Boise and Soldier mtns. These higher elevations will see liquid total range between 0.5-1.0" through Thursday night with amounts tipping toward the higher end of that range across the southern Boise/Soldier mtns. Lesser amounts are expected across the w-central ID mtns roughly north of the Payette River. While southerly flow provides steadier precipitation in the mtns, valleys will see breaks during this time. Snow levels will run between 3.5-4.5 kft MSL across SE Oregon and 4-5.5 kft across SW Idaho through the period, with Thursday on the upper end of those ranges. This will result in rain through Thursday evening across most lower elevation valleys including the Snake Plain. It won't be until late Thursday night that a mix or change over to snow will occur as the upper low passes to our east allowing colder air to filter in.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Unsettled conditions continue as the upper-level low moves east of the area Friday, bringing northwesterly flow aloft and light showers. With snow levels expected to be around 3000-3500 ft MSL before the precipitation moves out, valley wintry mix and mountain snow is currently forecast. Precipitation will gradually taper off through the day Friday. The pattern will continue to evolve quickly thereafter, with a shortwave upper- level ridge Saturday providing dry conditions until the next strong low pressure system begins to moves on shore late Saturday. Southwesterly flow aloft will move over the region with increasing precipitation chances Saturday night and lasting through Monday. Another brief upper-level ridge is well agreed upon long range models late Monday into early Tuesday before another system moves in and brings widespread precipitation chances yet again. Temperatures will hover near or slightly below normal in SW Idaho and 5-10 degrees below normal in SE Oregon through the period. Breezy winds will accompany systems passing through.

BOU.name: Boulder / Denver
BOU.excerpt: After Saturday, ensemble guidance is in good agreement that below normal temperatures and on and off precipitation chances look to continue through much of next week.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - First wind event of the season likely (>70%) for the northern Front Range mountains and foothills late tonight into Wednesday. Gusts of 60-75 mph with isolated stronger gusts possible.
- Brief potential for wind gusts of 40-50 mph and isolated stronger wind gusts for the Hwy 93 corridor (Boulder to Golden) and northern Weld County.

- Critical fire weather conditions for the southern Front Range foothills and Palmer Divide on Wednesday. Elevated fire weather conditions possible across the northern Front Range mountains, foothills, and adjacent plains.
- Chance for mountain snow late tonight into Wednesday morning. Another event likely Friday into Saturday.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: Today has been a pleasant day with high temperatures topping out in the upper 50s for the majority of the plains. A trough currently located over Nevada will approach Colorado tonight and move through on Wednesday. This will bring some snow to the central and northern mountains tonight and into Wednesday morning. The Park Range continues to look most favored for 2-4 inches of snow. Our central and northern mountains are forecast to see a dusting to perhaps an inch or two of snow. Modeling has trended to a slight increase in moisture leading to the slight bump in snowfall totals. Some briefly moderate to heavy snow is possible overnight given steep lapse rates.

Wednesday is shaping up to be an impactful day for the majority of our area. Some ingredients appear increasingly likely to come into place for a Bora event producing high winds. Subsidence and cross barrier, near-westerly flow of 50-60 kts looks likely. Our area will be in the right exit region of the jet in the morning before the jet is nearly overhead by Wednesday afternoon. Some high-resolution model soundings continues to show a stable layer/inversion in the 600 to 700 mb range, which would help to enhance the already strong winds.

Gusty winds look to first begin in the northern mountains as early as 11pm tonight. Stronger winds should slowly spread to the east into the northern foothills as we progress through Wednesday morning. Wind gusts between 60 and 75 mph are expected with perhaps a few gusts stronger than that at the highest peaks in the northern Front Range mountains and foothills. DESI REFS probabilities highlight this potential well with increasing probabilities (50-70% chance) of gusts >70 mph with the greatest chances for locations above 9,000 feet. We have upgraded to a High Wind Warning in these locations from 11pm Tuesday through 11am Wednesday.

As of now, high-resolution model guidance shows the peak of the winds along the Hwy 93 corridor- Boulder to Golden- between 7am and noon Wednesday. There is increased confidence compared to yesterday of a slightly stronger surface pressure gradient and stronger momentum transfer. This would introduce a few hour window of wind gusts of 40-50 mph with the potential for some isolated locations seeing slightly stronger wind gusts in this corridor. These stronger winds could possibly extend as far east as KBJC to KLMO, but there is uncertainty on how far east the strongest winds could make it. Once we reach late Wednesday morning into the afternoon, areas along our far northern tier, including the I-25 corridor north of Fort Collins, could see gusts of 40-50 mph with some isolated stronger wind gusts possible. As is typical in these setups, narrow channels of 30 to 45 mph wind gusts could extend to the east across southern Weld County and in the southern Denver metro. 18z modeling shows the potential for a secondary push of stronger wind gusts along the Hwy 93 corridor early Wednesday afternoon as cold air advection continues, but this scenario remains rather uncertain. In addition, we have continued to trend dewpoints lower given the increased subsidence for Wednesday morning and afternoon. Elevated to critical fire weather conditions are expected. See the Fire Weather Discussion for more details.

Thursday will feature a much calmer weather pattern with weak ridging aloft. High temperatures will remain in the mid to upper 50s for the plains. The next storm system will move into the area on Thursday night into Friday. A trough will once again move in, but take a slightly more southerly and slower track compared to Wednesday's trough. A few shortwaves associated with the trough will bring precipitation chances on Friday and Saturday to our area. The highest confidence of any snowfall accumulations remains for our central and northern mountains given the flow aloft. As we get into Friday night and Saturday morning, some light rain showers are possible with perhaps a few snowflakes making it into the lower elevations. These chances remain rather unimpressive- only about 20- 30% of ensemble guidance shows any sort of light dusting. We do note that the last few runs of both the ECMWF and GFS deterministic models do try to bring some flakes into the Denver metro on Saturday morning as a surface low develops and brings light upslope winds to the area. As previously noted, this will be a period to keep an eye on.

After Saturday, ensemble guidance is in good agreement that below normal temperatures and on and off precipitation chances look to continue through much of next week. This should finally bring us our first prolonged taste of some cooler temperatures to the lower elevations!

CYS.name: Cheyenne
CYS.excerpt: Tuesday...As the shortwave trough aloft moves across early in the day, expect scattered rain and snow showers, with drying noted in the afternoon as a low amplitude shortwave ridge aloft transitions overhead.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - The first notable high wind event of the season is on track Tuesday evening through Wednesday. High Wind Watches and Warnings are in effect.
- Wind gusts of 60 to 75 mph are expected in the typical wind prone areas along Interstates 80 and 25, with gusts up to 65 mph possible in adjacent zones.
- Expect a quick hitting round of rain and snow showers in Carbon and western Albany Counties tonight.
- Near critical fire weather conditions are possible Wednesday afternoon in portions southeast Wyoming and western Nebraska. A Fire Weather Watch is in effect.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: The next 36 hours will be rather busy, with the passage of a cold front bringing precipitation chances, strong winds, and of course, cooler temperatures. The remainder of the afternoon will be relatively pleasant with mild temperatures. However, winds will begin to increase out west as an upper-level trough swings into Wyoming this evening. At roughly the same time the trough arrives in Wyoming, precipitation will begin to move into western Carbon County. The cold front will be somewhat delayed behind the precipitation, so precipitation will initially start as rain for the lower elevations of Carbon County. Colder air will arrive later in the evening, allowing any remaining precipitation in Carbon and Albany Counties to transition to snow. Accumulations outside of the mountains are not anticipated. Even the mountains are not likely to pick up more than a few inches of snow with this being a quick and progressive trough. Most precipitation will dissipate by midnight, as winds turn more westerly behind the front, drying out the environment.

As previously mentioned, the frontal passage this evening will cause winds to increase overnight. Some changes were made this forecast package in regards to wind headlines, mainly upgrades to Watches, extending the Warning area and adding a few more Watches. Behind the front, MSLP gradients will rapidly compress, allowing winds to quickly strengthen. CAG to CPR height gradients, both 850 and 700 mb, are over 70 meters, signifying a strong wind event for the Arlington zone. These strong gradients will cause winds aloft to increase, eventually maxing out at 70 to 80 kts over the Laramie Range. Very strong subsidence will also exist over the wind prones, co-located with the strongest winds aloft, meaning that it is very likely that these winds make it down to the surface. Given the 750 mb 80 kt bullseye over the North Laramie Range with the strong downward omega, included the North Laramie Range in a High Wind Warning as gusts of 75 MPH will be possible. Upgraded the High Wind Watches for Converse and central Laramie County to Warnings as cross sections of omega and potential temperature show a strong mountain wave signature. Breaking mountain waves could easily cause 65+ MPH gusts in these locations. In-house guidance also has about 40 percent chances for hitting high winds in these locations. A bit more uncertainty exists west of the Laramie Range. Hi-Res guidance like the HRRR is excited about high winds, as is the GFS LAMP, which can be a decent predictor of high winds. The NBM still isn't as bullish with putting high winds in the Laramie Valley and Shirley Basin, so for the time being, added both of these zones to a High Wind Watch. Early Wednesday morning into early Wednesday afternoon will be the most likely timeframe to see the strongest winds. The wind prone areas and the North Laramie Range are expected to see the highest gusts, with 75 MPH gusts possible. Areas in Watches and Warnings outside of the wind prones could see gusts to 65 MPH. The rest of the CWA will also be quite windy with gusts over 50 MPH expected. As the trough ejects out of Wyoming Wednesday afternoon, winds will weaken as MSLP gradients rapidly relax.

High temperatures on Wednesday will drop 10 to 15 degrees behind the front compared to Tuesday. This will put temperatures in the 40s and low 50s for most locations. Despite the cooler temperatures, fire weather concerns will still be prevalent due to the high winds. Downsloping winds off the Laramie Range will create dry conditions from the Interstate 25 corridor eastward into the southern Nebraska panhandle. Here, relative humidity will range from 15 to 20 percent, borderline critical conditions. However, because the winds will be very strong, control problems are likely and fires could spread rapidly. Therefore a Fire Weather Watch has been issued for Wednesday afternoon for the area mentioned above. Once the winds die down, the overnight hours look relatively uneventful with near average low temperatures.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Thursday...Another relatively mild day is expected with strong southwest flow aloft and the paucity of low and mid level moisture. 700 mb temperatures near 3 Celsius will help produce maximum temperatures in the mid 40s to lower 50s. Low level gradients suggest a breezy day.

Friday...Even stronger southwest flow aloft prevails with a decent shortwave trough aloft moving across central Wyoming, producing synoptic and orographic snows for Carbon County and the Snowy and Sierra Madre Ranges, and dry conditions elsewhere. Breezy to windy based on low and mid level gradients.

Interestingly, this date, the 20th of November marks the latest first measurable snowfall of 0.1 inches or greater in the autumn at Cheyenne, and it looks as if we will likely eclipse this record, with no measurable snowfall at Cheyenne through November 20th.
Saturday...The split shortwave trough aloft moves across the Rockies with drying conditions noted for our counties in the afternoon.
Sunday...Ridging aloft moves overhead with westerly flow aloft over our counties. Again, the atmosphere looks too dry for any precipitation development.

Monday...In this progressive pattern, the next shortwave trough aloft moves into western Wyoming, spreading orographic snows across our Snowy and Sierra Madre Ranges, though amounts look minimal, with dry conditions elsewhere.

Tuesday...As the shortwave trough aloft moves across early in the day, expect scattered rain and snow showers, with drying noted in the afternoon as a low amplitude shortwave ridge aloft transitions overhead.

GJT.name: Grand Junction
GJT.excerpt: Cold air in the wake of this system will keep afternoon highs below normal through the extended forecast, with morning lows below freezing. The latest freeze on record for Grand Junction's Walker Field sits at November 26th.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Rain and snow will taper across the mountains early Wednesday morning. Motorists can expect slick roads on mountain passes.
- Winds will taper some overnight, but remain gusty into the morning hours of Wednesday as this system exits.
- Temperatures will trend downward late week, with colder air delivering the first freezing temperatures for some desert valleys.
- Another storm will bring measurable snowfall to the mountains Friday and Saturday.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: Rain and snow showers will continue to work across the Divide early Wednesday morning, as the storm system lifts out onto the Plains. Mountain passes will remain slippery overnight, but drier conditions and clearing skies will improve road conditions by mid day Wednesday. Clouds will begin to clear out in the afternoon and temperatures will only recovery slightly as we remain a few degrees below normal. Winds will remain gusty against the Divide through the morning, then lighten from southwest to northeast as the upper level winds subside.

A brief transitory ridge moves overhead Thursday, pushing temperatures back up a few degrees. Unfortunately, clouds will begin to invade again, ahead of a low diving out of the PACNW into the Great Basin. Winds will begin to pick up again across the Four Corners on Thursday, as a strong jet streak rounds the base of the low digging into the Great Basin. By Thursday afternoon, the Uncompahgre and San Juans will see gusty winds too. Thursday evening, another plume of moisture will work into northeast UT and northwest CO, with rain and snow showers developing. Snow levels drop into the 6-7k neighborhood Thursday night and continue to lower Friday, with most of the CWA below freezing by Saturday morning. Mountain snow will pick up in the Uintas Thursday night and spread southeast across the CO mountains through Saturday morning. A few low valleys might see a dusting by Saturday morning, should cold air hold with this system. Otherwise, it looks like some of the best snow will favor the central mountains of Colorado. This forecast could vary as the track of the low adjusts, but for now it looks like a broad swath of 6-8 inches of mountain snow and locally higher totals on favorable aspects.

Cold air in the wake of this system will keep afternoon highs below normal through the extended forecast, with morning lows below freezing. The latest freeze on record for Grand Junction's Walker Field sits at November 26th. In an anomalously warm and wet fall, it looks like this record will live on another year thanks to the arrival of cold air in the valley with this storm. High pressure moves across the region late this weekend and starts off Thanksgiving week. Models are hinting at another disturbance crossing the region Tuesday, with perhaps, the beginnings of another unsettled period for the holiday weekend. More on that to come in subsequent forecast packages.

PUB.name: Pueblo
PUB.excerpt: As the system moves through, the area will cool off considerably, with cool and mild conditions lasting into early next week.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Quick-moving system tonight into early Wednesday, with mountain snow showers and gusty winds area-wide.
- Another system will move in Thursday Night, bringing more gusty winds and snow to the San Juans through Saturday.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Temperatures will continue to warm through the rest of the day today, with mid-60s over the plains and 50s over the valleys. Gusty winds will pick up across the area this afternoon as well, mainly out of the southwest. Gusts 45-50 mph will be possible, strongest along the KS border and over the eastern half of the San Luis Valley. Gusts up to around 60 mph are expected over the peaks of the mountains.

Tonight, a quick-moving upper wave will pass through the area. Showers will push into the mountains from the west, dropping a few inches of snow over the peaks while the lower elevations remain dry. Gusty winds will also persist across the area, with peak gusts a bit before midnight before they start to weaken again early Wednesday morning. Strong gusts will linger the longest over the eastern mountains.

Overall, snow accumulations with this system have generally trended down over the last few days, though today's guidance has showed a bit more variability in the amplitude of the passing trough. In general, the central mountains and the Sangres will see an inch or less, though snow totals over the San Juans and parts of the La Garitas have varied more considerably. As of now, the southwest mountains should be getting widespread 3-5 inches by Wednesday afternoon, though local amounts could be as high as 6-8 inches. Some of the CAMs have shown the potential for a foot or more, and while it can't be ruled out due to orographic forcing, it's a low-end chance.

The passing wave quickly moves east of us tomorrow, taking the best forcing with it. As it departs, snow showers will come to a quick end over the mountains as winds continue to weaken. Though slightly cooler air will be in place, bringing highs down a few degrees, spill expecting temps in the 40s-50s over the valleys, while the plains mix up into the low-mid 60s.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Thursday still looks mild and dry. Cloud cover will decrease, with high temperatures in the 50s-60s over most of the CWA. We'll still see some gusty south winds over the plains and the San Luis Valley, but gusts will generally stay below 35 mph or so.

Our next system will move in, starting Thursday Night and lasting into Saturday. Snow amounts have continued to trend down with the last few rounds of model solutions, though today's guidance shows the main axis of the incoming trough moving through Colorado through the day on Saturday. Once again, the heaviest snow will fall over the San Juans, with long-range guidance remaining consistent around the 3-6 inches mark for accumulations. Gusty winds will also make a return to most of the area, though the peak winds will largely depend on the strength of the system as it moves through. Some of these winds may be on the stronger side, though considerations for any highlights will need to wait until forecast confidence increases, since there is still some variation in the strength of the system between models.
As the system moves through, the area will cool off considerably, with cool and mild conditions lasting into early next week.

SLC.name: Salt Lake City
SLC.excerpt: With colder air spreading into the region late this week, freezing temperatures will be possible around the St George and Zion Canyon areas Friday and Saturday nights.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Winter Weather Advisories remain in effect for the Wasatch and western Uinta Mountains, along with the Wasatch Back, where additional accumulating snow is expected.

- Another storm system will bring significant mountain snow Thursday into Friday, with snow levels falling near to below 5000 feet by Friday. Another 6 to 12 inches of mountain snow, with locally higher amounts near 2 feet for the upper Cottonwoods is expected in northern Utah, while 4 to 10 inches of mountain snow is forecast for central and southern Utah.
- Freezing temperatures are increasing in probability for the Virgin River corridor near Zion National Park Saturday and Sunday mornings.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: An energetic, negatively tilted shortwave trough continues to lift through northern Utah/far southwest Wyoming this evening. While the better forcing is shifting north and east of the forecast area, orographically enhanced snowfall will persist across northern Utah through the remainder of the evening before diminishing overnight. Thus far any enhancement from the GSL has been minimal, however the potential remains as -10C 700mb temperatures remain over the area. Large scale subsidence in the wake of the ejecting trough will bring and end to any lingering precipitation overnight, and have adjusted the going Winter Wx Advisories to end at 4am across the north, while canceling the remaining advisory for southern Utah.

Shortwave ridging will bring a temporary drying trend Wednesday as a cool and more stable airmass settles across the forecast area. Max temperatures will remain in the 40s across most northern/western valleys Wednesday afternoon, running roughly 5 degrees below climo.

The next upper trough to impact the region will make landfall along the Pacific Coast on Wednesday, then gradually spread inland and cross the Great Basin/Intermountain Region during the Thursday/Friday timeframe. Unlike the current trough, this late- week system will come through in a more piecemeal fashion. The initial surge of moisture advection will arrive Thursday, however this plume will be cresting the Sierra which will block a substantial amount of moisture from penetrating further inland. A portion of this upper trough is forecast to eject across the region Thursday night into early Friday, followed by the larger scale trough axis Friday night into early Saturday. As such, widespread heavy precipitation looks unlikely during this timeframe, but when all is said and done the northern mountains are looking at another 6-12" (locally higher) with a half inch of QPF in the valleys. Colder air with the main trough axis Friday will lower snow levels to the valley floors of northern Utah with some accumulation possible, particularly along the benches. Precipitation across southern Utah will remain largely focused on the Thurday-Thursday night window, thus lower precip totals are expected.

With colder air spreading into the region late this week, freezing temperatures will be possible around the St George and Zion Canyon areas Friday and Saturday nights. On the topic of freezing temperatures, KSLC fell to 32 degrees this evening, which tied the date of the latest first fall freeze on record (2021 and 2016).

2660.travel_advice: Heightened avalanche conditions on specific terrain features. Evaluate snow and terrain carefully; identify features of concern.

product.author: Mike Walter
bottom_line: Avalanche danger at higher elavtions will rise on Wednesday as new snow and increasing wind will deposit wind-drifted snow onto a weak snow surface. You'll find this recent wind-loading near and above treeline on slopes facing west through north to east.
Below treeline the conditions are generally safe due to thin or non-existent snow cover.

2745.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Ian Fowler
bottom_line: Most slopes are safe and lack sufficient coverage for an avalanche. At high elevations, steer clear of isolated patches of firm, drifted snow below ridges or in steep gullies.

2842.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

product.author: Kevin Studley
bottom_line: Winter has begun to embrace the West Central Mountains of Idaho. 6-12 inches of new snow has fallen between Friday the 13th and Monday the 16th. Another 6-12 inches could stack up by the end of the week. If you're traveling in the mountains this week, watch out for wind slabs 1-2 feet thick above 7,000 feet and pay attention to terrain traps.
We'll update the General Avalanche Information weekly until full-time forecasting operations begin.
hazard_discussion: From 60-degree temperatures to over a foot of new snow, the weather sure has changed quickly over the past week. A cooler and wetter weather pattern has taken shape over our region since Friday the 13th. As of Monday (16th) afternoon, some mountain locations have picked up 6-12 inches of new snow along with southerly winds gusting 20-30 MPH.
Wind Slabs
• Wind slabs could become reactive this week with over a foot of new snow and gusty winds. Wind slabs will be most sensitive just below ridgelines.
• Look for clues of wind-affected snow, such as drifts, dunes, pillows, and freshly built cornices.
• Watch for signs of instability, such as shooting cracks. If you're observing these signs, find another aspect away from wind-drifted snow.
• Strong winds and local terrain features can alter the prevailing wind direction. Pay attention to cross-loading and wind-loading on unsuspecting slopes.
Early Season Conditions
• If you're out hiking or hunting in the mountains this fall, stay tuned to changing weather conditions. Avalanches are most likely during and immediately after a storm.

• Keep in mind the adage, "If there's enough snow to ride, there's enough snow to slide". Even if there's not enough snow to bury you, a small slide over uncovered logs, rocks, and brush would not be a fun way to start the season.
• Stay up to date on mountain weather with our WEATHER tab, where you'll find webcams, weather stations, and weather forecasting tools.
Check Your Winter Gear

• Beacons, shovels, probes, airbags. Run through all your gear and make sure it's functioning properly. Does your transceiver or airbag need any firmware updates? Look for cracks, defects, or corroded batteries. Make it fun with your friends and do a pre-season gear check with your winter travel companions.
Continuing Education
• Check out the Education tab on our website to sign up for avalanche courses this winter (COURSES ).
• Stay tuned to our EVENTS pages for other local happenings with the winter community.
• Interested in attending a snow and avalanche workshop (SAW)? Check out A3's WEBSITE for a list of events.
Observations
• Keep an eye on our observation page HERE

• If you're out in the mountains, submit an observation HERE. Early season observations help forecasters and the public alike. A simple photo and/or weather observation helps paint the picture of where snow is and where it is not.

Yeah, that's right: the Payette Avalanche Center has a new website. Browse around before the snow starts flying. We're also on the Avy App. You can search for "Avy: Avalanche & Weather Info" in your app store on your mobile device.

product.author: Mike Walter
bottom_line: Increasing winds and new snow will raise the likelihood of encountering pockets of stiffer, wind-blown snow at higher elevations. These isolated wind drifts could produce small avalanches.
